A rapid tall-to-athletic bilateral descent followed by a static no-rebound finish defines this card; no flight or external height is required.
Athletic, landing, and control labels name the same action, while stance, arm start, depth, speed, and hold time are variant or dose dimensions.
The card is a bilateral land-and-squat preparation pattern without a required aerial phase.
Jump, rebound, unilateral, box, depth-drop, and moving-entry tasks remain separate definitions.
Rapid ankle, knee, and hip flexion control organizes the descent while foot, frontal-plane, transverse-plane, and trunk control stabilize the finish.
The listed muscles describe contributing roles and do not claim isolation or exact activation magnitude.
Landing instruction and feedback can alter measured landing mechanics, but direct transfer to this exact no-flight snap-down has not been established.
The quality contract therefore records whole-foot pressure, knee-foot alignment, trunk control, contact sound, and a motionless finish without claiming injury prevention.

Exercise complexity rises with faster descent, more demanding arm starts, deeper target positions, stricter alignment, and longer stick criteria; physical difficulty remains modest without flight or external load.
Overall exercise difficulty equals the greater of complexity and physical difficulty; athlete proficiency is not an exercise-card field.
Load is bodyweight through a bilateral closed chain with rapid eccentric control and a low contact budget.
Dose stays quality-limited and ends before descent speed, contact sound, alignment, breathing, or finish control changes.
Use a flat dry nonslip floor, overhead clearance, a marked personal station, and direct observation.
Do not add a box, drop height, rebound, or conditioning density to this identity.
Use short sets of fully reset repetitions with a declared two-to-three-second stick and ample rest.
Exact repetitions and scores are programming proposals pending calibration rather than externally validated prescriptions.
Declare stance, arm start, target depth, repetitions, hold time, quality gate, and stop signal before starting.
Reach tall, snap down, organize the whole foot and knee, freeze without rebound, breathe, and reset.
Stop for symptoms, giving way, uncontrolled contact, repeated knee or trunk collapse, extra steps, breath holding, fear, or unsafe floor conditions.
A failed stick is recorded rather than hidden or converted into another repetition.
Use as low-impact landing-shape preparation before more demanding jump, sprint, or deceleration work when it improves the session task.
Do not use completion of this drill alone as proof of readiness for high-impact activity.
Athlete support names expected effort, unexpected symptoms, self-checks, access options, and nonvideo instruction.
The athlete reports symptoms, fear, loss of pressure, or a failed stick immediately.
Coach support covers front and side observation, fault correction order, demonstration, group spacing, and exact recording.
The coach reduces speed before increasing depth or volume and stops for persistent faults or symptoms.
A slower drop, shallower depth, hands-at-chest start, visual floor marker, fewer repetitions, or longer reset can improve access.
A slow Drop Squat to Stick is a separate regression identity rather than silently changing the rapid snap-down contract.
Arm position and depth are modifiers; athletic, landing, and control names are the same identity.
Slow drop squats, jumps, rebounds, unilateral finishes, and external-height tasks require separate definitions.

claims: A leader and follower face each other in a bounded lane; the follower responds to the leader's live body movement using lateral shuffle footwork without contact.
Drill, partner, box, and lane labels do not add an action; a preplanned route removes the defining perception-action coupling.
The task is reactive lateral locomotion with live visual cueing and planned spatial boundaries.
Crossover, sprint exit, tag, ball, resistance, hopping, crawling, and ladder tasks remain separate definitions.
Hip, knee, ankle, foot, and trunk actions repeatedly accelerate and brake the body laterally while maintaining frontal- and transverse-plane control.
The card makes no muscle-isolation or exact force-distribution claim.
Live opponent information couples perception and movement selection, distinguishing reactive agility from preplanned change of direction.
Evidence supports that distinction, but exact outcome magnitude for this mirror-shuffle format is not established.
Complexity rises with leader unpredictability, response speed, lane width, stricter accuracy, and role switching; physical difficulty rises with speed, braking force, round length, and density.
Overall exercise difficulty equals the greater of complexity and physical difficulty; athlete proficiency belongs only to skill-library cards.
Repeated lateral accelerations and braking load the adductors, lateral hip, quadriceps, calves, trunk, and attention.
End the round before accuracy, spacing, footwork, posture, or braking quality declines.
Use a flat dry nonslip bounded lane, matched partners, declared roles, no contact, and enough separation from other pairs.
Do not run the task when spacing, footwear, floor conditions, or partner behavior is unsafe.
Use short accurate rounds with complete role rotation and enough rest to preserve reading and braking quality.
Exact round duration, accuracy threshold, and score remain calibration proposals.
Declare lane, roles, spacing, allowed shuffle-only footwork, round time, accuracy target, stop signal, and role-switch rule.
The follower reads the partner's body, moves laterally without crossing the feet, preserves spacing, and brakes inside the lane.
Stop for symptoms, collision risk, repeated foot crossing, loss of spacing, uncontrolled braking, guessing, boundary violations, or partner mismatch.
Regress to a preplanned lateral walkthrough when live cueing prevents safe mechanics.
Use fresh after lateral mechanics when live perception-action coupling serves the session objective.
Do not default to conditioning density or use a solo preplanned shuffle under this identity.
Athlete support explains both roles, expected lateral and attention effort, self-checks, nonvideo instruction, and how to report unsafe speed or symptoms.
The athlete reports missed reads and unsafe spacing rather than guessing faster.
Coach support covers pairing, cue behavior, spacing, stance, first step, foot crossing, braking, accuracy, role balance, and group traffic.
The coach reduces leader speed or lane demand before extending round duration.
A slower leader, narrower lane, shorter round, larger spacing, stronger visual contrast, or rehearsed first round can improve access.
A preplanned walkthrough is a distinct regression identity because it removes live perception-action coupling.
Lane size, round time, speed, spacing, and role order are modifiers; partner and drill names are the same identity.
Preplanned, crossover, sprint-exit, pursuit/contact, implement, obstacle, or alternate-locomotion tasks require separate definitions.

claims: A planned straight-line acceleration transitions through a declared braking zone into a controlled bilateral athletic stick without a cut, turn, or reacceleration.
Five-yard and seven-to-ten-yard approaches are exact distance variants because they change entry speed and braking demand, not the accelerate-brake-stick sequence.
The card combines linear locomotion and planned horizontal deceleration with a bilateral static finish.
Reactive cues, multidirectional cuts, backpedal entries, resistance, run-through finishes, and reacceleration remain separate definitions.
Foot, ankle, knee, hip, and trunk actions absorb and redirect forward momentum through repeated braking contacts.
The listed muscles describe contributors to braking and stabilization without claiming isolation.
Horizontal deceleration requires braking force, eccentric capacity, posture control, and multi-step organization; achieved entry velocity materially changes demand.
Exact card distances and dose thresholds are programming proposals rather than directly validated prescriptions.
Complexity rises with approach speed, braking precision, shorter zones, and stricter stick criteria; physical difficulty rises with entry velocity, hard braking contacts, and density.
Overall exercise difficulty equals the greater of complexity and physical difficulty; exercise cards do not classify athlete proficiency.
Short acceleration plus multi-step braking creates substantial eccentric and impact demand in the quadriceps, calves, gluteals, hamstrings, adductors, and trunk.
Track hard braking events and end before run-throughs, panic steps, twisting stops, alignment loss, or declining entry intent.
Use a flat dry high-traction surface, measured approach and braking zones, clear runout, one-way lanes, and one athlete per lane.
Do not prescribe a speed or braking zone the athlete cannot repeatedly own.
Use low numbers of fully recovered quality events, count hard braking contacts, and cap cumulative sprint, impact, and braking budgets.
The longer approach carries higher physical difficulty and requires repeatable success at the shorter variant first.
Declare approach distance, start stance, entry intent, braking zone, finish mark, stick time, repetitions, lane order, and stop signal.
Accelerate straight, lower under control before the line, use ordered braking steps, stop without twisting, and hold the finish.
Stop for symptoms, giving way, panic steps, run-through, twisting, repeated alignment loss, unsafe traffic, surface failure, or inability to stop inside the zone.
Reduce intent or extend the braking zone before adding repetitions.
Use fresh in movement-learning or early output work before fatigue-heavy lower-body training.
Do not hide the braking dose inside conditioning or combine it with untracked high-speed running.
Athlete support explains the lane, expected braking effort, self-checks, symptoms, confidence reporting, and how to reduce speed safely.
The athlete reports a run-through, twist, panic step, or fear rather than forcing the target speed.
Coach support covers measuring zones, traffic flow, posture, braking onset, foot sequence, stop location, stick quality, and cumulative exposure.
The coach reduces intent or returns to the shorter distance when braking is not repeatable.
Lower intent, a shorter approach, longer braking zone, fewer events, longer rest, and high-contrast markings can improve access.
A lower-speed eccentric stop is a distinct substitution when the athlete cannot yet own acceleration entry.
Five-yard and seven-to-ten-yard approaches are variants; intent, zone length, stance, and hold time are modifiers.
Cuts, reactive cues, reacceleration, backpedal entries, resistance, and run-through finishes require separate definitions.

claims: Repeated low-amplitude unilateral ankle-dominant contacts without an intentional inter-repetition stick define this card.
Support and travel direction are selectable variants; bilateral contacts, higher projected bounds, terminal sticks, obstacles, loads, and linked actions remain separate definitions.
The card is a unilateral repeated-contact jump pattern with sagittal action plus frontal- and transverse-plane control.
Stationary, forward-traveling, and lateral-line variants preserve repeated contacts while changing support or landing location.
Foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk coordinate repeated unilateral spring contacts, with high local demand at the foot-calf-Achilles complex.
Muscle roles are not isolation claims, and exact tissue loading cannot be inferred from the label alone.
Unilateral and bilateral hopping produce different stiffness behavior, supporting a distinct laterality contract.
Exact cadence, amplitude, direction, dose, readiness threshold, and score for these variants are not directly validated.
Complexity rises when hand support is removed or the landing location travels; physical difficulty rises with unsupported contacts, speed, amplitude, direction, density, and accumulated impact.
Overall exercise difficulty equals the greater of complexity and physical difficulty; athlete proficiency remains a skill-library concept.
Every landing contact counts toward unilateral impact and foot-calf-Achilles volume, with secondary knee, hip, and trunk control demand.
End the set before contact sound or time, heel behavior, landing location, alignment, height, cadence, support use, or symptoms change.
Use a flat dry nonslip surface, adequate footwear, marked personal space, clear travel lanes, and a stable support only for the supported variant.
Do not use through pain, swelling, giving way, unsafe balance, poor landing tolerance, or untracked same-session impact.
Dose by quality contacts per side with declared cadence, amplitude, direction, rest, and cumulative impact budget.
Exact contact counts, recovery windows, and difficulty scores remain review and calibration proposals.
Declare side, support, direction, line or lane, contact count, cadence, amplitude, arm action, finish rule, rest, and stop signal.
Stay tall and springy, return the foot to the declared location, keep quick quiet contacts, and do not insert a stick between repetitions.
Stop for symptoms, swelling, giving way, heel slam, loud or slow contacts, landing drift, knee or pelvis collapse, altered cadence, excessive support, or unsafe surface.
Reduce contacts or return to supported or bilateral work when quality cannot be restored.
Use fresh in lower-leg, landing, sprint, or jump preparation when repeated unilateral contacts serve the objective.
Count every contact and avoid post-fatigue impact density or untracked overlap with running and jumping.
Athlete support explains expected foot-calf effort, unexpected symptoms, contact self-checks, side reporting, access options, and nonvideo instruction.
The athlete reports contact deterioration or Achilles-area symptoms immediately.
Coach support covers side balance, support use, foot return, sound, contact time, heel behavior, knee-pelvis-trunk alignment, travel path, and cumulative contacts.
The coach reduces direction or support demand before adding contacts, amplitude, or density.
Stable light hand support, fewer contacts, lower cadence, smaller amplitude, stationary placement, longer rest, or a high-contrast line can improve access.
Bilateral pogo is a separate laterality identity rather than an undeclared modification.
Supported stationary, unsupported stationary, linear-forward, and lateral-line tasks are exact variants; cadence and contact count are modifiers.
Bilateral, terminal-stick, hop-and-stick, bound, obstacle, loaded, reactive, and linked sprint or jump tasks require separate definitions.
